article.overview: An electron spectrometer measures the energy, and in many designs the arrival direction, of low-energy electrons in space or at a planetary surface. Three lunar-related examples are documented in this article: the Apollo 14 Charged Particle Lunar Environment Experiment (CPLEE), which measured electrons and ions at the lunar surface [1][2]; the Lunar Prospector Electron Reflectometer (ER), which measured solar wind electrons reflected from lunar crustal magnetic fields from orbit [4][5]; and the ESA-S1 and ESA-S2 electron analysers of the SELENE (Kaguya) Plasma energy Angle and Composition Experiment (PACE) [7][8].
article.description:
An electron spectrometer is typically built around an electrostatic analyser. Electric fields steer electrons of a chosen energy through the instrument to a detector, so that counts can be sorted by energy and, where the design allows, by direction of arrival. The lunar examples differ in viewing geometry. CPLEE had two analysers, one pointing towards local lunar vertical and one pointing 60 degrees from vertical towards lunar west [1][2]. The Lunar Prospector ER used a disk-shaped 360-degree field of view on a spinning spacecraft [4][5]. PACE measured electrons and ions with dedicated sensors, and its ESA sensors are specified with an angular resolution of 5 degrees by 8 degrees [8].

Electron spectrometers are distinct from ion spectrometers, which measure heavier charged particles. Several lunar plasma instruments combine both, as CPLEE and PACE do [2][8].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Electron measurements address three main questions. First, electrons in the solar wind and in the Earth's magnetotail form part of the plasma environment that reaches the Moon; low-energy electron and ion measurements at the surface were a stated purpose of CPLEE [2]. Second, electrons reflected from the lunar surface can probe magnetic fields in the crust. The Lunar Prospector MAG/ER experiment was designed to investigate the origin and nature of lunar crustal magnetic fields and to constrain the size of a metallic core [4][5]. Third, electron energy and angle distributions near the Moon help characterise how the lunar environment interacts with the solar wind. PACE was built to measure the three-dimensional distribution of low-energy electrons and ions around the Moon [7][8]. The relevance of electrons to surface charging is recognised, but this article does not quantify it because no verified value was obtained in this run.
article.operating_principle:
A typical electrostatic electron analyser applies voltages to electrodes so that only electrons within a narrow energy band reach the detector. Stepping the voltage builds up an energy spectrum, and the geometry of the analyser or a deflection system provides angular information. Detection is usually by electron multipliers or an imaging detector.

The CPLEE used two electrostatic analysers. Each had five small-aperture electron multipliers and one large-aperture electron multiplier. In automatic mode the instrument cycled every 19.2 seconds through 18 energy windows per analyser [2]. The Lunar Prospector ER used a symmetric hemispherical electrostatic analyser that focuses particles onto an imaging detector [4][5]. The PACE ESA sensors have a stated energy range of 5 eV to 15 keV and an angular resolution of 5 degrees by 8 degrees, with a 1-second sampling interval [8].
article.scientific_importance: Electron measurements matter because electron populations shape part of the lunar plasma environment, and because electrons reflected from the surface carry information about local magnetic fields that images alone cannot reveal. The Lunar Prospector ER was paired with a magnetometer to investigate the origin of lunar crustal magnetic fields and to constrain the size of a metallic core [4][5]. CPLEE provided low-energy electron and ion measurements from the lunar surface during the Apollo era [1][2]. PACE extended electron and ion measurements to lunar-orbit observations as part of SELENE [7][8]. The examples show one measurement type serving surface, orbital and magnetic-field science, but they were built for different missions and should not be treated as one standard instrument.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for an electron spectrometer. The values below describe three specific instruments and their stated sources. Where a value is shared with another instrument, or where sources disagree, this is stated.

examples.name: Apollo 14 Charged Particle Lunar Environment Experiment (CPLEE)
examples.type: Historical instrument flown as part of the Apollo 14 ALSEP on the lunar surface
examples.full_external_dimensions: Not found in the sources read.
examples.energy_range: 40 eV to 20 keV for electrons and ions
examples.analyser_configuration: Two electrostatic analysers; each with five small-aperture and one large-aperture electron multiplier; 18 energy windows per analyser; automatic mode cycle 19.2 s.
examples.deployment: Deployed about 3 m northeast of the ALSEP central station at approximately 18:00 UT on 5 February 1971; dust cover removed 19:30 UT on 6 February 1971.
examples.operating_history: Analyser B power supply failed 8 April 1971; analyser A partial power-supply failure 6 June 1971; intermittent operation in 1972; continuous operation December 1972 to February 1973; standby when ALSEP shut down 30 September 1977.
examples.qualification: Mass, power and operating-history values come from a Wikipedia summary; the primary PDS instrument document was identified but not read in this run.

examples.name: Lunar Prospector Electron Reflectometer (ER)
examples.type: Lunar orbital instrument on the Lunar Prospector spacecraft
examples.mass_kg: about 5 (combined with MAG; no ER-only value in label)
examples.power_w: about 4.5 (combined with MAG; no ER-only value in label)
examples.sensor_type: Symmetric hemispherical electrostatic analyser, based on the Mars Global Surveyor instrument, modified for a spinning spacecraft; focuses particles onto an imaging detector.
examples.energy_range: Low-resolution product: 15 energy bins from about 40 eV to 20 keV, over 16 spacecraft rotations (about 80 s). No instrument-level range stated in label.
examples.boom_placement: ER and electronics box at the ends of a small cross bar on the MAG/ER boom, about 1 m inboard from the MAG; MAG about 2.6 m from the spacecraft bus.
examples.data_products: ER_3D calibrated spectra 1998-01-16 to 1999-07-29; DATAL2 derived electron reflection data 1998-06-08 to 1999-06-27.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The three instruments differ widely in form. CPLEE is specified by a stowed volume of 2540 cm3 without full external dimensions. The Lunar Prospector ER sensor is a 12 cm diameter, 9 cm high cylinder within a shared MAG/ER package. The PACE ESA cross-section figure carries a 10 cm length marking, but no overall PACE dimension was found.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: CPLEE is stated at 2.7 kg. The Lunar Prospector MAG and ER together are about 5 kg; no ER-only mass was found. PACE mass was not found in the sources read.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: CPLEE: 3.0 W normal operation, 6.0 W at night with the survival heater on. Lunar Prospector MAG and ER together: about 4.5 W. PACE power was not found in the sources read.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Lunar-surface electron spectrometers operate in vacuum, with large temperature swings and exposure to radiation. CPLEE illustrates the thermal problem: its power rose from 3.0 W to 6.0 W at night when the survival heater was on [2]. Its operation was also limited by power-supply and voltage problems [2]. The Lunar Prospector ER had to be adapted from its Mars Global Surveyor design for a spinning spacecraft [4][5]. Electrostatic analysers need stable high voltages and clean electron detection, and their pointing and mounting affect what they measure. These are engineering considerations. The sources read do not quantify them for any example in this article.
article.limitations: Electron energy and angle values depend on calibration and on the instrument design. The PACE electron energy range is given differently in different sources [7][8]. The Lunar Prospector mass and power figures are shared with the magnetometer [5]. The CPLEE values rest on a secondary summary [2]. An electron spectrometer measures electrons only, so ion species require separate sensors, as in PACE [8]. A single station or spacecraft cannot by itself locate a source without comparison data.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Surface electron spectrometers would be delivered as part of a lander or surface experiment package. Orbital electron spectrometers would be integrated into a lunar-orbit spacecraft. No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument with its host spacecraft or lander on Earth.
Launch and transfer to the Moon.
Surface payloads: land, deploy, level, thermally protect and connect power and data.
Orbital payloads: insert into lunar orbit, commission, and operate with pointing, thermal and data interfaces.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: CPLEE was deployed by astronauts as part of the Apollo 14 ALSEP package, about 3 m northeast of the central station [2]. The Lunar Prospector ER was mounted on a boom on a spinning spacecraft [4][5]. Deployment for PACE was not verified in this run.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 14 CPLEE (surface, astronaut-deployed) [2]; Lunar Prospector ER (orbital, boom-mounted) [4][5]; SELENE PACE (lunar orbit) [7][8].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: Compatibility of a new electron spectrometer with any lander or spacecraft must be assessed from verified mass, dimensions, mounting, loads, power and data interfaces. The SwRI MAPS plasma spectrometer was described in 2023 as delivered for a lunar lander, but its electron capability is not stated and it is not assigned to a lander here [6].

article.historical_significance: CPLEE was one of the Apollo-era ALSEP experiments. It operated from 1971 until ALSEP was shut down on 30 September 1977, with degraded performance for much of that period [2]. The Lunar Prospector ER, together with the MAG, contributed to the investigation of lunar crustal magnetic fields [4][5]. PACE, on SELENE, has an in-flight performance and initial results paper published in 2010 [7].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Values for these instruments are not interchangeable. The CPLEE mass, power and operating history rest on a secondary summary [2] rather than the primary instrument document [3], which was identified but not read in this run. The Lunar Prospector mass and power figures are shared with the magnetometer [5]. The PACE electron energy range differs between the JAXA specification table [8] and the 2010 paper summary [7], and its mass and power were not found. These gaps mean this article is a rerun draft of the example set, not a complete engineering comparison.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. The one verified image is repeated in its section-level array. The CPLEE and Lunar Prospector examples have no verified direct image URL, so no image is listed for them.

data_quality_notes: v2 rerun. The reason for the correction was not supplied; the v1 files (electron_spectrometer_payload_121.md/.json/.urls.txt) were left untouched and were not compared line by line.

CPLEE mass, power, stowed volume and operating history come from a Wikipedia summary. The primary PDS instrument document (a14a_cplee.pdf) was identified but its text could not be read with the available tools.
Lunar Prospector ER mass (about 5 kg) and power (about 4.5 W) are combined values with the MAG; no ER-only values were found.

PACE electron energy range conflicts: JAXA specification table 5 eV to 15 keV for ESA; summary of Saito et al. 2010 gives 6 eV to 9 keV (ESA-S1) and 9 eV to 16 keV (ESA-S2). The 2010 paper was not opened (redirect to a login page).
PACE mass, power and external dimensions were not found. Mission dates for SELENE and Lunar Prospector launch details were not verified in this run.
SwRI MAPS (2023 press release) is not counted as an electron spectrometer because the release does not state whether it measures electrons, ions or both.
Image coverage is limited: one image verified (JAXA PACE sensor figure). No verified direct image URLs were obtained for CPLEE or the Lunar Prospector ER.
